title: Camp 3 close: your practice
hookLine: a morning bow, a sitting, a walk, metta, the precepts, a gift, the holy days
last: KATHINA — THE RAINS END IN GIFTS.

cards: On day ninety-seven, camp three began with four short phrases: may you be safe, may you be happy, may you be healthy, may you live with ease.

Since then you've sat with sixteen steps of the breath, walked a lane of twenty paces, taken the refuges, met the five precepts, given without a receipt, bowed three times, lit a candle, kept the holy days, and learned what a retreat is.
That's a lot of practice. Today it all gathers into something you can actually keep.

teach.b: Camp three was built to add up: a morning, an evening, a week and a year. The morning, built on day one hundred forty-four: a bow, the homage, the breath, a wish of metta, and a dedication of whatever good was done.
Ten minutes. The evening: metta for sleep, kindness sent out in six directions, or a short sitting of your own, with the hindrances named when they visit.

teach.h: A WEEK: WALK, PRECEPTS, A GIFT.
teach.b: The week holds the rest. A walk that's also a practice, on the lane or on the way to the bus. The five precepts, kept as trainings and taken again whenever one slips.
A gift, small and wholehearted, with no receipt. And maybe, now and then, a quiet half-day at home.

The year is the holy days: Vesak in May, Asalha Puja in July, the rains retreat and its three-month practice, kathina in the autumn, Magha Puja in February or March. The tradition has a pair of words for all this.
Pariyatti is learning the teaching: reading, listening, studying. Patipatti is practicing it: sitting, keeping precepts, giving.
Camp two was mostly stories, camp three mostly practice. Tomorrow, camp four turns to the text itself: the Dhammapada, a book of the Buddha's sayings in verse, read in order, one piece a day.
The practice doesn't stop there. Each day's verse comes with a sit and a line to carry, so the words have somewhere to land. You already know how to sit.
You know how to bow, walk, give, and begin again.

how: Many lay Buddhists keep a simple daily rhythm, such as bowing and chanting at a home shrine in the morning, sitting or metta in the evening, the five precepts through the week, giving to the monastery, and the major holy days through the year.

o: realization: the final insight at the path's end
practice: actually doing the teaching, day by day
study: reading and learning the teaching's texts

games.q: match each piece of camp three to where it fits.

s: pariyatti means studying the teaching and patipatti means practicing it
the tradition pairs them: learning and doing.
once the reading of the Dhammapada starts, the sitting stops
each day of camp four keeps a sit and a line to carry.
a good practice plan is the most heroic one you can imagine
keep it realistic: what you can actually keep through busy weeks.

games.q: you've written a plan: an hour of sitting every morning. by day three you've missed twice. what fits what camp three taught?
o: give up; it isn't for you.
shrink the plan and begin again.
double it to make up the time.
games.why: the precepts are trainings, taken again and again. a small plan you keep beats a big one you drop.

practice: With a pen, or just in your mind, sketch your week: which pieces of the morning practice you'll keep; metta, a sitting, or both in the evening; a walk, a gift and one precept somewhere in the week; one holy day in the year.
Keep it realistic, not heroic. When the sketch feels right, put it down and sit with the breath, the way you've done a hundred times now.

wordCard.voice: Patipatti. Practice, the doing of the teaching: a morning, an evening, a week and a year of it, gathered into something you can keep.

orig.note: Pali: practice, the doing of the teaching, paired with pariyatti, its study.

carryVoice: Your line: you can do this. A small plan you keep beats a big one you drop. Camp three, complete.
